What's new in emergency medicine

Authors:
:   [Michael Ganetsky, MD](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/contributors)
:   [Jonathan S Grayzel, MD](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/contributors)
:   [James F Wiley, II, MD, MPH](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/contributors)

All topics are updated as new evidence becomes available and our [peer review process](/home/editorial-policy) is complete.

Literature review current through: Jul 2026.

This topic last updated: Aug 04, 2026.

Please read the [Disclaimer](#disclaimerContent) at the end of this page.

The following represent additions to UpToDate from the past six months that were considered by the editors and authors to be of particular interest. The most recent What's New entries are at the top of each subsection.

ADULT RESUSCITATION

Anticoagulation in extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (July 2026)

Data guiding anticoagulation during extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) are limited. In a recent randomized trial of 330 patients (60 percent venoarterial ECMO, 40 percent venovenous ECMO), low-dose [unfractionated heparin](/contents/heparin-unfractionated-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) (UFH) resulted in a nonsignificant reduction in severe bleeding compared with standard-dose UFH (58 versus 65 percent), without increasing severe thromboembolic complications (11 versus 10 percent) [[1](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/1)]. Although promising, interpretation is limited because the standard-dose regimen may not reflect current practice, anti-factor Xa monitoring was inconsistent and the study was open label. More robust data are needed before we can routinely use low-dose UFH for anticoagulating ECMO patients. (See ["Extracorporeal life support in adults: Management of venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA ECMO)", section on 'Anticoagulation'](/contents/extracorporeal-life-support-in-adults-management-of-venoarterial-extracorporeal-membrane-oxygenation-va-ecmo?sectionName=Anticoagulation&topicRef=8365&anchor=H372499665&source=see_link#H372499665).)

Liberal versus restrictive oxygenation targets after cardiac arrest (June 2026)

The optimal peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2) target in mechanically ventilated cardiac arrest survivors is uncertain. In a recent randomized trial of 1840 such patients targeting an SpO₂ of 95 percent with an allowable minimum fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO₂) of 0.21 resulted in similar rates of favorable functional outcomes, mortality, and length of stay at 180 days compared with higher oxygen targets and allowable minimum FiO₂ of 0.3, without and increase in adverse events [[2](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/2)]. These data support our practice of targeting an SpO2 at the lower end of the 95 to 98 percent range. (See ["Intensive care unit management of the intubated post-cardiac arrest adult patient", section on 'Airway, ventilation, and oxygen targets'](/contents/intensive-care-unit-management-of-the-intubated-post-cardiac-arrest-adult-patient?sectionName=Airway%2C+ventilation%2C+and+oxygen+targets&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3262398353&source=see_link#H3262398353).)

Catheter-directed thrombolysis versus anticoagulation in pulmonary embolism (March 2026)

In patients with intermediate-high-risk pulmonary embolism (PE; ie, biochemical and imaging evidence of right ventricle [RV] dysfunction), limited data suggest that catheter-directed thrombolysis improves RV function compared with anticoagulation alone, but does not improve mortality. In a recent randomized trial of 544 patients with intermediate-high-risk PE, ultrasound-facilitated, catheter-directed thrombolysis with [alteplase](/contents/alteplase-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) reduced the composite outcome of PE-related death, cardiorespiratory decompensation, or symptomatic PE recurrence compared with anticoagulation alone (4 versus 10 percent); this difference was driven primarily by fewer episodes of decompensation (3.7 versus 10.3 percent) [[3](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/3)]. Major bleeding was numerically higher in the alteplase group (4 versus 2 percent) but was not statistically significant, and the difference in RV size at 48 hours between the two groups was also not significant. Interpretation is limited by low event rates, lack of blinding, and underrepresentation of patients >75 years. However, these data support our practice of performing catheter-directed therapies in patients with intermediate-high-risk PE. (See ["Acute pulmonary embolism in adults: Reperfusion therapy in intermediate- and high-risk patients", section on 'Catheter-directed thrombolysis'](/contents/acute-pulmonary-embolism-in-adults-reperfusion-therapy-in-intermediate-and-high-risk-patients?sectionName=Catheter-directed+thrombolysis&topicRef=8365&anchor=H4140125415&source=see_link#H4140125415).)

Updated international Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines (March 2026)

The Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines have recently been updated [[4](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/4)]. The guidelines suggested that, while a mean arterial pressure of 65 mmHg should be targeted, a range of 60 to 70 mmHg is practical for most adults with sepsis. The guidelines also emphasized the importance of screening tools for early detection and management of sepsis, while discouraging both overly aggressive fluid resuscitation and empiric treatment for fungal and anaerobic bacterial infections, especially when suspicion is low. The guidelines encouraged active fluid removal (in the later phases of shock), rapid de-escalation of antimicrobials and, in mechanically ventilated patients, the use of selective digestive tract decontamination to prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia. We agree with these recommendations. (See ["Evaluation and management of suspected sepsis and septic shock in adults", section on 'Introduction'](/contents/evaluation-and-management-of-suspected-sepsis-and-septic-shock-in-adults?sectionName=INTRODUCTION&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1&source=see_link#H1).)

Joint European and United States definition of refractory septic shock (March 2026)

Although sepsis and septic shock have widely accepted definitions, there has not been consensus regarding the definition of "refractory" septic shock. The Society of Critical Care Medicine and European Society of Intensive Care Medicine have recently proposed criteria defining refractory septic shock by the presence of (1) persistently elevated lactate concentration (>2 mmol/L [>18 mg/dL]) and/or prolonged capillary refill time, (2) lack of response to fluid resuscitation, (3) a norepinephrine base equivalent dose >0.5 micrograms per kilogram per minute, and (4) in those with suspected mixed shock, critical care ultrasound should be used to confirm lack of response to fluids and to exclude other etiologies for shock [[5](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/5)]. The impact of this definition on patient outcomes, such as survival, remains undetermined. (See ["Sepsis syndromes in adults: Epidemiology, definitions, clinical presentation, diagnosis, and prognosis", section on 'Septic shock'](/contents/sepsis-syndromes-in-adults-epidemiology-definitions-clinical-presentation-diagnosis-and-prognosis?sectionName=Septic+shock&topicRef=8365&anchor=H8&source=see_link#H8).)

High-flow oxygen does not affect mortality in hypoxemic respiratory failure (March 2026)

Although frequently used, the value of high-flow oxygen delivered via nasal cannulae (HFNC) in patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure remains unclear. In a randomized trial of 1110 such patients, HFNC did not reduce 28-day mortality compared with low-flow oxygen [[6](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/6)]. HFNC led to a non-significant reduction in the intubation rate at 28 days (42.4 versus 48.4 percent), and rapidly improved patients' respiratory rates, dyspnea, and carbon dioxide levels. These data support our practice of administering HFNC only to patients with advanced oxygen needs (eg, >6 L/minute) rather than routine administration. (See ["Evaluation and management of the nonventilated, hospitalized adult patient with acute hypoxemia", section on 'Humidified, high-flow oxygen delivered via nasal cannulae (HFNC)'](/contents/evaluation-and-management-of-the-nonventilated-hospitalized-adult-patient-with-acute-hypoxemia?sectionName=Humidified%2C+high-flow+oxygen+delivered+via+nasal+cannulae+%28HFNC%29&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3611214250&source=see_link#H3611214250).)

ENVIRONMENTAL EMERGENCIES

Iloprost for amputation prevention in frostbite (May 2026)

[Iloprost](/contents/iloprost-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) is a prostacyclin analog that is indicated for the treatment of grade 3 or 4 frostbite (ie, cyanosis that extends proximal to the distal phalanx after rewarming), but supporting evidence is limited. In a study with over 250 patients (80 receiving iloprost) in two Canadian regions that differed in routine iloprost use but with a standardized frostbite care pathway, iloprost was associated with a lower amputation rate for grade 3 frostbite (30 versus 53 percent) but not for grade 2 and 4 frostbite; patients receiving a higher total iloprost dose were less likely to have amputations [[7](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/7)]. In 40 patients with grade 4 frostbite, iloprost treatment was associated with fewer finger and toe segment amputations (40 versus 51 percent and 47 versus 58 percent, respectively). These findings support our recommendation for iloprost in patients with severe frostbite. (See ["Frostbite: Acute care and prevention", section on 'Iloprost within 72 hours'](/contents/frostbite-acute-care-and-prevention?sectionName=Iloprost+within+72+hours&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1902794625&source=see_link#H1902794625).)

Microorganisms in children with freshwater drowning-associated pneumonia (February 2026)

Infection with gram-negative organisms, especially *Aeromonas* species, is predominantly reported in patients with drowning-associated pneumonia (DAP). In a study from China of over 70 children with freshwater DAP in a pediatric intensive care unit, *Staphylococcus aureus* was the most isolated organism [[8](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/8)]. Other common pathogens included *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*, *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, *Klebsiella pneumoniae*, *Candida albicans*, and rhinovirus. These findings highlight the need for an empiric broad-spectrum antibiotic regimen, including coverage of gram-positive bacteria, in children with suspected DAP. (See ["Drowning (submersion injuries)", section on 'Pneumonia'](/contents/drowning-submersion-injuries?sectionName=Pneumonia&topicRef=8365&anchor=H809358478&source=see_link#H809358478).)

Effectiveness of defibrillation in patients with hypothermia and nonperfusing shockable rhythm (February 2026)

Patients with hypothermia and nonperfusing shockable arrhythmias are less likely to have return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) with defibrillation at a core temperature <30°C (86°F). Current recommendations are to attempt defibrillation with up to three shocks but withhold further attempts pending rewarming since cold myocardium can potentially be injured. A registry-based study with almost 40 patients with cardiac arrest, a shockable rhythm, and core temperature <30°C found that ROSC was more likely if defibrillation was performed during rewarming, as compared with before rewarming (100 versus 25 percent) [[9](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/9)]. Defibrillation during extracorporeal life support (ECLS) had a fivefold increase in odds of ROSC. These findings support our recommendations to attempt defibrillation even with temperature <30°C and to not withhold defibrillation during ECLS rewarming at temperature >25°C (77°F). (See ["Accidental hypothermia in adults: Management", section on 'Ventricular arrhythmias or asystole'](/contents/accidental-hypothermia-in-adults-management?sectionName=Ventricular+arrhythmias+or+asystole&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1808505299&source=see_link#H1808505299).)

Acute hypersensitivity reactions from rattlesnake antivenom in alpha-gal endemic region (February 2026)

CroFab and Anavip, antivenoms used to treat Crotalinae snakebite envenomation, can potentially cause severe allergic reactions. Anavip contains more of the carbohydrate moiety galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose (which is responsible for alpha-gal syndrome) compared with CroFab. A study with over 200 patients in Arkansas (a state with a high rate of alpha-gal sensitization) who received either Anavip or CroFab found that Anavip was associated with increased adverse drug reactions (including presumed anaphylaxis) compared with CroFab (22 versus 4 percent) [[10](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/10)]. Basophil activation testing from individuals with known alpha-gal syndrome found that Anavip more potently activated alpha-gal sensitized basophils. Clinicians who treat snakebite victims in regions with high rates of alpha-gal sensitization must be ready to manage anaphylaxis following antivenom (especially Anavip) administration. (See ["Bites by Crotalinae snakes (rattlesnakes, cottonmouths [water moccasins], or copperheads) in the United States: Management", section on 'Acute antivenom hypersensitivity reactions'](/contents/bites-by-crotalinae-snakes-rattlesnakes-cottonmouths-water-moccasins-or-copperheads-in-the-united-states-management?sectionName=Acute+antivenom+hypersensitivity+reactions&topicRef=8365&anchor=H4098260420&source=see_link#H4098260420).)

GENERAL ADULT EMERGENCY MEDICINE

YEARS criteria for pulmonary embolism exclusion in patients with active cancer (July 2026)

The YEARS criteria adjusts D-dimer cutoffs for excluding pulmonary embolism (PE) based on pretest probability, but it is unknown whether it can be utilized in patients with active cancer. In a randomized trial including 698 patients with active cancer suspected of having a PE, the diagnostic failure rate at 90 days was similar in patients evaluated by the YEARS algorithm compared with a standard chest computed tomography pulmonary angiogram (1.8 versus 5 percent) [[11](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/11)]. Limitations of the study included an open-label design, exclusion of patients with a life expectancy <3 months, lack of subgroup analysis by cancer site and stage, and early cessation of the study. Nonetheless, these results suggest that YEARS may be used to exclude PE in patients with active cancer, although further study and validation is needed. (See ["Clinical presentation and diagnostic evaluation of the nonpregnant adult with suspected acute pulmonary embolism", section on 'Alternative (adjusted) D-dimer cutoffs with or without YEARS'](/contents/clinical-presentation-and-diagnostic-evaluation-of-the-nonpregnant-adult-with-suspected-acute-pulmonary-embolism?sectionName=Alternative+%28adjusted%29+D-dimer+cutoffs+with+or+without+YEARS&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2075009429&source=see_link#H2075009429).)

Cyclosporiasis outbreak in the United States (July 2026)

Cyclosporiasis is a parasitic infection characterized by watery diarrhea, usually caused by ingestion of contaminated food. In May 2026, a large outbreak of cyclosporiasis was recognized in the United States [[12](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/12)]. The source of the cases appears to be related to the ingestion of a widely distributed contaminated lettuce product [[13](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/13)]. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention advises clinicians to consider cyclosporiasis in the diagnosis of patients presenting with watery diarrhea, ask the laboratory to specifically test stool for Cyclospora spp. (with PCR, if available), and ask patients with suspected or confirmed cyclosporiasis about their recent food and travel history. Up-to-date information on the cyclosporiasis outbreak in the United States can be found on the [CDC cyclosporiasis page.](/external-redirect?target_url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.cdc.gov%2Fcyclosporiasis%2Fphp%2Fsurveillance%2Findex.html&token=t7NCXpgOToFkdCMjAwY9q6i4%2BvYZVJy0risdHMpqEf106dXhWudmk2P8tRKy0awIS4MtcwKnOZ3Rcfrqurs4668AtSQsFLDSFqHlsS1NKKs%3D&TOPIC_ID=8365) (See ["*Cyclospora* infection", section on 'Epidemiology'](/contents/cyclospora-infection?sectionName=EPIDEMIOLOGY&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2&source=see_link#H2).)

Marine toxin disease outbreaks in the United States (July 2026)

Marine toxins are an important cause of noninfectious foodborne disease outbreaks. Scombroid poisoning causes flushing, a warmth sensation, and an erythematous, urticarial rash often prominent on the face and upper torso soon after ingestion of improperly stored fish. Ciguatera poisoning causes a gastrointestinal illness followed by delayed onset neurologic symptoms such as paresthesias and temperature-related dysesthesias. A study of the United States Foodborne Disease Outbreak Surveillance System found that 402 marine toxin outbreaks were reported between 2011 and 2023, representing 1280 affected individuals; nearly all outbreaks implicated scombroid or ciguatoxin [[14](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/14)]. These findings underscore the need to inquire about recent fish consumption in patients presenting with characteristic clinical features and may help inform public health surveillance and prevention efforts. (See ["Scombroid (histamine) poisoning", section on 'Epidemiology'](/contents/scombroid-histamine-poisoning?sectionName=EPIDEMIOLOGY&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1057420&source=see_link#H1057420) and ["Ciguatera fish poisoning", section on 'Epidemiology'](/contents/ciguatera-fish-poisoning?sectionName=EPIDEMIOLOGY&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3603702&source=see_link#H3603702).)

American Thoracic Society guidelines on noninvasive respiratory support (July 2026)

The American Thoracic Society (ATS) recently issued guidelines on the use of noninvasive respiratory support for patients with acute respiratory failure, in whom low-flow oxygen is insufficient [[15](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/15)]. The ATS recommends using high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) oxygen for acute hypoxemic respiratory failure and suggests noninvasive ventilation (NIV) for acute hypercapnic respiratory failure. The ATS also suggests either modality for preoxygenation prior to endotracheal intubation; post-extubation, the ATS suggests HFNC for low-risk patients and NIV for high-risk patients. We agree with these recommendations. (See ["Evaluation and management of the nonventilated, hospitalized adult patient with acute hypoxemia", section on 'Oxygen and respiratory support'](/contents/evaluation-and-management-of-the-nonventilated-hospitalized-adult-patient-with-acute-hypoxemia?sectionName=Oxygen+and+respiratory+support&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1642231459&source=see_link#H1642231459) and ["Noninvasive ventilation in adults with acute respiratory failure: Benefits and contraindications"](/contents/noninvasive-ventilation-in-adults-with-acute-respiratory-failure-benefits-and-contraindications?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) and ["Extubation management in the adult intensive care unit"](/contents/extubation-management-in-the-adult-intensive-care-unit?topicRef=8365&source=see_link).)

Fosphenytoin for trigeminal neuralgia attacks (May 2026)

Several pharmacologic options are available to treat acute trigeminal neuralgia (TN) pain, but available supporting evidence is limited. In a randomized trial that included 22 patients with acute TN symptoms, pain reduction on the numerical rating scale (0 for no pain up to 10 for worst pain) was greater at two hours among those assigned to [fosphenytoin](/contents/fosphenytoin-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) than placebo (-6.1 versus -2.4) [[16](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/16)]. Treatment consisted of a loading dose followed by once daily maintenance treatment for up to four days. Patients assigned to fosphenytoin also had a higher rate of >50 percent pain reduction and reduction in the frequency of attack recurrence, and treatment was generally well tolerated. These data provide clinical trial evidence to support the role of fosphenytoin for acute TN exacerbations. (See ["Trigeminal neuralgia", section on 'Acute rescue therapy for patients with breakthrough pain'](/contents/trigeminal-neuralgia?sectionName=Acute+rescue+therapy+for+patients+with+breakthrough+pain&topicRef=8365&anchor=H372586115&source=see_link#H372586115).)

AHA/ACC guidelines for pulmonary embolism (March 2026)

Several societies, including the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC), have issued joint guidelines for the evaluation and management of pulmonary embolism (PE) [[17](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/17)]. The guidelines stratify patients by risk of PE-related death to facilitate management. Patients in category A (incidental PE), B (symptomatic PE with a low clinical severity score), and C (symptomatic PE with an elevated clinical severity score) require anticoagulation. Patients in category D (incipient cardiopulmonary failure) and E (cardiopulmonary failure) are candidates for reperfusion therapies (eg, thrombectomy or thrombolysis, if they have a low bleeding risk). We await adoption of this classification and encourage its use to facilitate management. (See ["Acute pulmonary embolism in adults: Treatment overview and prognosis", section on 'American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology/others'](/contents/acute-pulmonary-embolism-in-adults-treatment-overview-and-prognosis?sectionName=American+Heart+Association%2FAmerican+College+of+Cardiology%2Fothers&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2148862999&source=see_link#H2148862999).)

GENERAL PEDIATRIC EMERGENCY MEDICINE

Pediatric sepsis hospitalization and mortality in the United States (March 2026)

New estimates of United States sepsis hospitalizations and in-hospital mortality based on a pediatric sepsis event definition derived from the 2024 Phoenix sepsis criteria have been reported using electronic-health record surveillance of clinical data from over 3.9 million pediatric hospitalizations (neonates excluded) from 2016 to 2023. The average annual hospital incidence of sepsis was 1.3 percent (over 18,000 annual cases); overall in-hospital mortality was 10.1 percent (over 1800 annual deaths) [[18,19](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/18,19)]. Annualized national estimates remained stable over the study period. These findings update prior sepsis estimates based upon older definitions of pediatric sepsis and confirm the high burden of pediatric illness due to sepsis in the United States. (See ["Sepsis in children: Definitions, clinical manifestations, and diagnosis", section on 'Burden of disease'](/contents/sepsis-in-children-definitions-clinical-manifestations-and-diagnosis?sectionName=Burden+of+disease&topicRef=8365&anchor=H632992306&source=see_link#H632992306).)

PEDIATRIC RESUSCITATION

International guidelines for the management of pediatric sepsis and septic shock (May 2026)

The 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Pediatric Guidelines for the management of sepsis and septic shock in children are available [[20](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/20)]. The guidelines reaffirm the prime importance of the rapid recognition of septic shock and treatment that includes timely administration of fluid bolus therapy, empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics, and, in patients not responding to fluid bolus therapy, initiation of vasoactive medications (epinephrine or norepinephrine) ([algorithm 1](/content-not-available)). The 2026 guidelines also provide new recommendations that promote the use of blood lactate trends, lung and cardiac point-of-care ultrasound, and central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO2 ≥ 70 percent) to monitor resuscitation. Our approach is consistent with these guidelines. (See ["Children with sepsis in resource-abundant settings: Rapid recognition and initial resuscitation (first hour)", section on 'Approach'](/contents/children-with-sepsis-in-resource-abundant-settings-rapid-recognition-and-initial-resuscitation-first-hour?sectionName=Approach&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2493912177&source=see_link#H2493912177).)

Balanced crystalloid solution versus normal saline for children with septic shock (April 2026)

For children with septic shock, whether to administer balanced crystalloid solutions (BCS; for example, [lactated Ringer](/contents/lactated-ringer-solution-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link)'s) versus normal [saline](/contents/sodium-chloride-preparations-saline-and-oral-salt-tablets-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) (NS) during initial fluid resuscitation is unclear. In a new randomized trial of over 8400 children with suspected septic shock, the combined outcomes of death, initiation of renal-replacement therapy, and persistent kidney dysfunction at 30 days were not significantly different in patients who were assigned to fluid resuscitation for up to 48 hours with BCS (3.4 percent) versus NS (3 percent) [[21](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/21)]. Hyperchloremia and hypernatremia were more common in patients receiving NS; increased blood lactate was more common in patients receiving BCS. Otherwise, adverse effects were similar in both groups. These findings suggest that either BCS or NS is an appropriate choice for fluid resuscitation of children with septic shock. However, the results may not be generalizable to patients with hospital-acquired sepsis or those treated in resource-limited settings. (See ["Children with sepsis in resource-abundant settings: Rapid recognition and initial resuscitation (first hour)", section on 'Fluid resuscitation'](/contents/children-with-sepsis-in-resource-abundant-settings-rapid-recognition-and-initial-resuscitation-first-hour?sectionName=Fluid+resuscitation&topicRef=8365&anchor=H19450206&source=see_link#H19450206).)

PRIMARY CARE ORTHOPEDICS AND SPORTS MEDICINE

Management of severely displaced distal radius fractures in children (April 2026)

For children with severely displaced distal radius fractures, the usual approach is fracture reduction and casting by a clinician or orthopedic surgeon with pediatric expertise. In a pragmatic trial of 750 children (4 to 10 years old) with severely displaced distal radial fractures, patients with markedly displaced Salter-Harris I or II physeal or metaphyseal fractures, were randomized to surgical reduction and casting versus casting alone [[22](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/22)]. At three months, functional outcomes, pain, and quality of life measured by validated scores as well as subjective cosmesis were significantly better in the surgical group. However, the difference in scores was small and less than minimally important differences for each outcome and became nonsignificant along with cosmesis at 12 months. These findings suggest that casting alone by an experienced clinician or orthopedic surgeon may be a reasonable option in children <10 years old with these injuries. However, we continue to support prompt reduction and casting pending further confirmation of these results. (See ["Distal forearm fractures in children: Initial management", section on 'Complete fracture'](/contents/distal-forearm-fractures-in-children-initial-management?sectionName=Complete+fracture&topicRef=8365&anchor=H34&source=see_link#H34) and ["Distal forearm fractures in children: Initial management", section on 'Displaced Salter-Harris I or II fractures'](/contents/distal-forearm-fractures-in-children-initial-management?sectionName=Displaced+Salter-Harris+I+or+II+fractures&topicRef=8365&anchor=H26&source=see_link#H26).)

Persistent symptoms of concussion in young children (March 2026)

In a prospective study, 235 young children (median age 2.4 years, 98 percent with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 15) were diagnosed with concussion in the emergency department (ED) based on the GCS score and ≥1 of the following: palpable skull fracture, headache (in verbal patients), altered mental status, or loss of consciousness [[23](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/23)]. At one month, 28 percent had persistent symptoms on a parent-reported symptoms score. This rate was significantly higher than in controls with orthopedic injuries undergoing ED evaluation and community children. On adjusted analysis, ED symptom severity was the primary predictor of persistent symptoms. These findings suggest that, similar to older children and adolescents, young children appear to have a significant risk of persistent symptoms of concussion after a mild head injury that appears to be associated with the severity of symptoms at initial evaluation. (See ["Concussion in children and adolescents: Management", section on 'Prognosis'](/contents/concussion-in-children-and-adolescents-management?sectionName=PROGNOSIS&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2832537&source=see_link#H2832537).)

Management of displaced medial epicondyle elbow fractures in children (January 2026)

For children with medial epicondyle elbow fractures, the degree of displacement that warrants operative intervention is debated. A multicenter pragmatic trial of 334 children with these fractures (24 percent with associated reducible elbow dislocations) randomly assigned patients to immobilization (typically cast or splinting) versus surgical treatment [[24](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/24)]. At 12 months after injury, functional outcomes, participation in sports and performing arts, pain, and quality of life were similar in the two groups; children assigned to surgery had more complications. These findings suggest that nonsurgical treatment is appropriate for most children with closed, displaced medial epicondyle elbow fractures. Surgical repair is still necessary for selected fractures complicated by an entrapped bony fragment in the elbow joint, ulnar nerve dysfunction, irreducible dislocation, or elbow instability. (See ["Epicondylar and transphyseal elbow fractures in children", section on 'Medial epicondylar fractures'](/contents/epicondylar-and-transphyseal-elbow-fractures-in-children?sectionName=Medial+epicondylar+fractures&topicRef=8365&anchor=H17&source=see_link#H17).)

PROCEDURES

POCUS in infants and young children undergoing transurethral bladder catheterization (July 2026)

Transurethral bladder catheterization (TUBC) is the preferred method for obtaining urine specimens for culture in infants and young children who are not toilet trained; visualization of urine in the bladder with point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) prior to TUBC may facilitate collection. In a meta-analysis of three trials (337 children undergoing TUBC), first attempt success rate was higher for patients undergoing POCUS (89.7 versus 72.5 percent) and the rate of catheterization attempts resulting in no urine present ("dry taps") was lower (3.6 versus 23.9 percent) compared with patients undergoing TUBC without POCUS [[25](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/25)]. These findings confirm improved success rates reported in prior studies and support routine use of POCUS prior to TUBC in this population whenever available. (See ["Urine collection techniques in infants and children with suspected urinary tract infection", section on 'Transurethral bladder catheterization'](/contents/urine-collection-techniques-in-infants-and-children-with-suspected-urinary-tract-infection?sectionName=Transurethral+bladder+catheterization&topicRef=8365&anchor=H678706983&source=see_link#H678706983).)

TOXICOLOGY

Severe hydrogen sulfide poisoning (June 2026)

Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) is a colorless gas with a rotten egg odor that potently inhibits mitochondrial respiration. It is a byproduct of microbial decomposition of organic matter (ie, "sewer gas") and various industrial processes. In a study of 168 patients with H2S poisoning reported to the Taiwan Poison Control Center, those working underground and in confined spaces were more likely to develop severe toxicity [[26](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/26)]. Early administration of [sodium nitrite](/contents/sodium-nitrite-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) was associated with potentially lower odds of death, but did not reach statistical significance. These findings should prompt clinicians to consider H2S poisoning in a patient with sudden loss of consciousness, lactic acidosis, and cardiovascular collapse who was working underground or in a confined space, and support our suggestion for treating these patients with sodium nitrite. (See ["Common occupational chemical exposures: General approach and management of selected exposures", section on 'Hydrogen sulfide'](/contents/common-occupational-chemical-exposures-general-approach-and-management-of-selected-exposures?sectionName=Hydrogen+sulfide&topicRef=8365&anchor=H394318957&source=see_link#H394318957).)

Poisoning-related fatality from illicit substances in children and adolescents (May 2026)

Illicit substances such as opioids can result in poisoning-related fatality in pediatric patients. In an analysis conducted on national surveillance databases from the Centers for Disease Control, the rate of death from poisoning (including illicit drug overdoses) in children and adolescents aged 1 to 19 years increased by 12.7 percent from 2020 to 2023 [[27](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/27)]. In 2023, 1913 deaths were from illicit drug overdoses, and the majority (79.5 percent) were from [fentanyl](/contents/fentanyl-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link). These findings confirm that illicit substances remain a common cause of fatality in children and adolescents, and that ongoing educational and other preventive measures are warranted in this population. (See ["Poisoning in children: Prevention", section on 'Fatalities'](/contents/poisoning-in-children-prevention?sectionName=Fatalities&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2&source=see_link#H2).)

Poisoning-related injury from ingested household products in young children (May 2026)

Ingested household products remain a common cause of poisoning-related injury in young children. An analysis of national surveillance data estimated that over 240,000 children aged ≤5 years were treated in United States emergency departments for injuries from exposure to household cleaning products from 2007 to 2022 [[28](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/28)]. Approximately 60 percent of injuries were from ingestion. The products and containers associated with the most injuries were bleach (30.1 percent), detergents (28.6 percent), detergent packets (33 percent), and spray bottles (28.2 percent). These findings highlight the importance of ongoing educational, regulatory, and product engineering measures to prevent injuries from ingested substances in pediatric patients. (See ["Poisoning in children: Prevention", section on 'Ingested substances'](/contents/poisoning-in-children-prevention?sectionName=Ingested+substances&topicRef=8365&anchor=H108484245&source=see_link#H108484245).)

Rome V diagnostic criteria for cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (April 2026)

Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS) is a clinical diagnosis. The Rome V criteria, which update the commonly used Rome IV criteria, were recently published [[29](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/29)]. A patient meets the Rome V criteria for CHS if all of the following are present:

●Stereotypical episodic vomiting resembling cyclic vomiting syndrome in terms of onset, duration, and frequency

●Presentation after prolonged (one year) and excessive cannabis use (≥4 days per week or ≥15 doses per week, or both)

●Relief of vomiting episodes by sustained cessation of cannabis use (at least six months or three typical emetic cycles)

Association with pathologic bathing behavior (prolonged hot baths or showers) is supportive but not necessary. We agree that these criteria can assist in diagnosing CHS. (See ["Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome", section on 'Diagnostic criteria'](/contents/cannabinoid-hyperemesis-syndrome?sectionName=Diagnostic+criteria&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3072534301&source=see_link#H3072534301).)

New recommendations on use of activated charcoal for overdoses (April 2026)

[Activated charcoal](/contents/activated-charcoal-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) (AC) adsorbs chemicals within minutes of contact, preventing gastrointestinal (GI) absorption and subsequent toxicity. Indications and timing are debatable, and "routine" use for GI decontamination has not demonstrated reduced morbidity and mortality in poisoned patients. Newly released recommendations from the Clinical Toxicology Recommendations Collaborative (which included representatives from three toxicology societies) suggest a potential benefit for a slightly prolonged window for AC administration for ingestion of certain agents (eg, [acetaminophen](/contents/acetaminophen-paracetamol-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link), salicylates, and [verapamil](/contents/verapamil-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link)) and an additional dose of AC for agents with potential for prolonged GI tract persistence (aforementioned agents as well as [carbamazepine](/contents/carbamazepine-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link), [valproic acid](/contents/valproate-valproic-acid-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link), paraquat, [phenobarbital](/contents/phenobarbital-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link), and [theophylline](/contents/theophylline-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link)) [[30](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/30)]. We agree with most of the recommendations from the Collaborative. (See ["Gastrointestinal decontamination of the poisoned patient", section on 'Indications'](/contents/gastrointestinal-decontamination-of-the-poisoned-patient?sectionName=Indications&topicRef=8365&anchor=H18993776&source=see_link#H18993776).)

Trends in kratom exposures reported to United States poison centers (March 2026)

Kratom (*Mitragyna speciosa*) is a natural product derived from a tree native to Southeast Asia used for its stimulant, analgesic, and antidepressant properties. Commercially sold kratom products can have alkaloidal concentrations that are different compared with natural leaf products, which can cause toxicity and dependence. There were over 14,000 kratom exposures reported to United States poison centers between 2015 and 2025 [[31](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/31)]. Reports steadily increased through 2019, plateaued through 2024, and surged in 2025 (over 3400 reported exposures). Reports involving multiple substances (eg, opioids) were more likely to cause serious outcomes and hospitalization. These findings suggest that kratom-related adverse effects are increasing in the United States. (See ["Kratom health effects from acute and chronic use", section on 'Epidemiology'](/contents/kratom-health-effects-from-acute-and-chronic-use?sectionName=EPIDEMIOLOGY&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2211216297&source=see_link#H2211216297).)

Chronic lead exposure and increased cardiovascular mortality (March 2026)

Cumulative lead exposure has been linked to an increased risk of atherosclerosis, cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality, and all-cause mortality. A study of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey from 1999 to 2014, including over 42,000 individuals, reported that higher estimated bone lead levels were associated with increased CVD mortality; the group with the greatest lead burden had an 88 percent increase in adjusted mortality risk compared with estimated preindustrial levels [[32](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/32)]. This corresponds to an estimated 3.5 million deaths globally in 2023 attributable to elevated bone lead levels, which would account for almost 6 percent of deaths and would make lead exposure the eighth leading risk for global mortality. These findings highlight the need to screen for and mitigate occupational and environmental lead exposure. (See ["Lead exposure, toxicity, and poisoning in adults: Clinical manifestations and diagnosis", section on 'Chronic and long-term exposure effects'](/contents/lead-exposure-toxicity-and-poisoning-in-adults-clinical-manifestations-and-diagnosis?sectionName=Chronic+and+long-term+exposure+effects&topicRef=8365&anchor=H7&source=see_link#H7).)

Causes and prognosis of acquired methemoglobinemia (March 2026)

Acquired methemoglobinemia is a potentially life-threatening condition in which the iron in heme becomes oxidized and cannot deliver oxygen. In a new study from Thailand that evaluated 169 individuals with acquired methemoglobinemia over a 10-year period, the most common causes were [dapsone](/contents/dapsone-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) (in 30 percent) and the contact herbicide propanil (in 27 percent, mostly for self-harm) [[33](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/33)]. Approximately 10 percent had glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. The fatality rate was 11 percent, 40 percent were admitted to the intensive care unit, 34 percent required intubation, and 89 percent were hospitalized. These data reinforce the importance of rapid recognition and treatment of this condition. (See ["Methemoglobinemia", section on 'Most common acquired causes'](/contents/methemoglobinemia?sectionName=Most+common+acquired+causes&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3113698015&source=see_link#H3113698015).)

Cardiotoxicity of supratherapeutic loperamide exposures (March 2026)

The antidiarrheal agent [loperamide](/contents/loperamide-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) has been reported to cause ventricular conduction disturbances, including QRS and QT interval prolongation, idioventricular rhythm, and ventricular tachycardia, following overdose. Loperamide is a synthetic opioid but does not typically cause classic signs of opioid toxicity. A systematic review of almost 130 cases of supratherapeutic loperamide exposure found that severe toxicity has been reported at daily doses as low as 20 to 40 mg [[34](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/34)]. Syncope was reported in almost half of cases, while severe cases mainly had polymorphic or sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. These findings suggest that patients with supratherapeutic loperamide exposure may benefit from cardiac monitoring. (See ["Acute opioid intoxication in adults", section on 'Loperamide'](/contents/acute-opioid-intoxication-in-adults?sectionName=Loperamide&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2282453505&source=see_link#H2282453505).)

Psilocybin use in Oregon and Colorado following decriminalization (March 2026)

Psilocybin is a hallucinogen found in many species of mushrooms and has been studied for the treatment of various mental health disorders. Psilocybin was decriminalized for use in licensed clinics in Oregon in 2020 and Colorado in 2022. A study of data from a national survey of drug use from 2018 to 2025 found that self-reported use increased in both states following decriminalization (mean prevalence increased from 2 to 4.5 percent and 2.7 to 4.3 percent in Oregon and Colorado, respectively) [[35](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/35)]. This increase was greater than a weighted composite control of the other states. These findings may impact policy decisions regarding psilocybin decriminalization for therapeutic use. (See ["Intoxication from LSD and other common hallucinogens", section on 'Epidemiology'](/contents/intoxication-from-lsd-and-other-common-hallucinogens?sectionName=EPIDEMIOLOGY&topicRef=8365&anchor=H57999532&source=see_link#H57999532).)

Test characteristics of an enzymatic ethylene glycol assay (March 2026)

Ethylene glycol poisoning is potentially fatal if not treated promptly. Diagnosis can be challenging since ethylene glycol concentrations are usually performed by gas chromatography, which is not widely available and typically has long turn-around times. A modification to a glycerol dehydrogenase-based assay approved for veterinary use has been externally validated and is used by some hospitals; it can be performed 24/7 and has a typical turn-around time of several hours. A study of over 400 samples analyzed by both an enzymatic assay and chromatography found a sensitivity and specificity of 89 and 83 percent, respectively [[36](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/36)]. All four false-negative enzymatic results were below the 20 mg/dL treatment threshold. These results suggest that an enzymatic ethylene glycol assay may be a valuable screening tool. (See ["Methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning: Pharmacology, clinical manifestations, and diagnosis", section on 'Testing for methanol and ethylene glycol'](/contents/methanol-and-ethylene-glycol-poisoning-pharmacology-clinical-manifestations-and-diagnosis?sectionName=Testing+for+methanol+and+ethylene+glycol&topicRef=8365&anchor=H12&source=see_link#H12).)

ED-initiated injectable extended-release buprenorphine (February 2026)

Previous studies have found that emergency department (ED) initiation of sublingual [buprenorphine](/contents/buprenorphine-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) is associated with decreased all-cause and opioid-related mortality and is feasible and cost-effective. A new trial with almost 2000 ED patients who had untreated opioid use disorder and signs of withdrawal found that ED patients started on extended-release injectable buprenorphine, compared with sublingual buprenorphine, had similar engagement in opioid use disorder treatment at 7 (41 versus 39 percent) and 30 days (44 versus 45 percent) [[37](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/37)]. The rate of precipitated withdrawal was similar and rare (<1 percent) in both groups despite a high prevalence of [fentanyl](/contents/fentanyl-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) dependence (76 percent). These results suggest that initiation of extended-release injectable buprenorphine may be a safe and feasible option in ED patients for treatment of an opioid use disorder. (See ["Acute opioid intoxication in adults", section on 'Prevention of recurrent opioid overdose'](/contents/acute-opioid-intoxication-in-adults?sectionName=PREVENTION+OF+RECURRENT+OPIOID+OVERDOSE&topicRef=8365&anchor=H10057659&source=see_link#H10057659).)

TRAUMA

Craniotomy for evacuation of intracranial epidural hematoma (July 2026)

Surgical evacuation is often performed in patients with large or symptomatic acute epidural hematomas (EDH) but the optimal surgical approach is uncertain. In an open-label, randomized clinical trial comparing craniotomy and craniectomy in 120 patients with acute traumatic EDH who had transtentorial herniation and a median injury-to-surgery time of 4 hours, favorable functional outcomes at six months were similar between groups (79 and 84 percent, respectively) [[38](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/38)]. Postoperative cerebral infarction and 30-day mortality rates were also similar between groups, but postoperative intracranial hemorrhage was more common in those assigned to craniectomy (36 versus 13 percent). The applicability of these data to patients with more delayed presentations and to those with EDH plus significant cerebral edema or other intracranial pathology is uncertain. These results support the use of craniotomy for surgical evacuation of EDH, even in the setting of transtentorial herniation. (See ["Intracranial epidural hematoma in adults", section on 'Surgical techniques'](/contents/intracranial-epidural-hematoma-in-adults?sectionName=Surgical+techniques&topicRef=8365&anchor=H13&source=see_link#H13).)

Capnography for prognosis in trauma patients (July 2026)

Studies have found that low end-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO₂) values in trauma patients on initial medical presentation may indicate a hemorrhagic state and be associated with increased mortality and transfusion requirements. In a meta-analysis with more than 2400 trauma patients, a low EtCO₂ was associated with higher mortality (22 versus 12 percent) and a greater need for transfusion (7 versus 1 percent) [[39](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/39)]. The definition of "low" EtCO₂ ranged from less than 26 to 35 mmHg across the studies, but was less than 30 mmHg in most. These findings suggest that a low EtCO2 may be a valuable, noninvasive early predictor of severity in trauma patients, but should be used in conjunction with other prognosticators (eg, vital signs, shock index, lactate). (See ["Carbon dioxide monitoring (capnography)", section on 'Increased ICP and trauma prognosis'](/contents/carbon-dioxide-monitoring-capnography?sectionName=Increased+ICP+and+trauma+prognosis&topicRef=8365&anchor=H11&source=see_link#H11).)

PECARN cervical spine injury prediction rule performance by patient age (May 2026)

In a planned subanalysis of the cohort of 22,430 children used to develop the Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network (PECARN) Cervical Spine Injury (CSI) prediction rule ([algorithm 2](/content-not-available)), age-specific rules were derived based on developmental transition (0 to <2 years, 2 to <8 years, 8 to <16 years, and 16 to <18 years) [[40](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/40)]. When compared with the PECARN CSI rule, testing characteristics were similar for the age-specific rules; the negative predictive value for the PECARN CSI rule (99.9 percent, prevalence of CSI 1.9 percent) equaled or exceeded all age-specific rules. These findings support the use of the PECARN CSI rule to determine the risk of CSI and the need for C-spine imaging in infants and children of all ages. (See ["Evaluation and acute management of cervical spine injuries in children and adolescents", section on 'Indications and choice of imaging'](/contents/evaluation-and-acute-management-of-cervical-spine-injuries-in-children-and-adolescents?sectionName=Indications+and+choice+of+imaging&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2844494741&source=see_link#H2844494741).)

Prehospital whole blood transfusion for traumatic hemorrhage (March 2026)

Two recent trials have examined the efficacy and safety of prehospital transfusion of low-titer, group O whole blood (LTOWB) versus blood components by Emergency Medical Services (EMS):

●In a pragmatic trial of over 600 patients with life-threatening bleeding transported by air ambulances in England, patients were transfused up to 2 units of LTOWB versus red cells plus plasma [[41](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/41)]. The composite of mortality plus massive transfusion within 24 hours and 90-day call-cause mortality was similar between the groups; the LTOWB group had slightly fewer serious adverse events.

●In another pragmatic trial of over 1000 patients with trauma and hypotension transported by air bases in the United States, either from the scene or from a referring emergency department, patients were transfused up to 2 units of LTOWB versus red cells, plasma, or both. Mortality at 30 days was similar (26 versus 21 percent) between LTOWB and components, as was in-hospital mortality, blood product requirements, and adverse events [[42](/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/42)].

These findings suggest that use of LTOWB, which is logistically simpler than components, is a reasonable option for EMS with prehospital transfusion programs. (See ["Initial management of moderate to severe hemorrhage in the adult trauma patient", section on 'Transfusion'](/contents/initial-management-of-moderate-to-severe-hemorrhage-in-the-adult-trauma-patient?sectionName=Transfusion&topicRef=8365&anchor=H749310297&source=see_link#H749310297).)

# Management of acute pulmonary embolism 2019: what is new in the updated European guidelines?

You have full access to this [open access](https://www.springernature.com/gp/open-science/about/the-fundamentals-of-open-access-and-open-research) article

## Abstract

Pulmonary embolism (PE) is the third most frequent acute cardiovascular syndrome. Annual PE incidence and PE-related mortality rates rise exponentially with age, and consequently, the disease burden imposed by PE on the society continues to rise as the population ages worldwide. Recently published landmark trials provided the basis for new or changed recommendations included in the 2019 update of the European Society of Cardiology Guidelines (developed in cooperation with the European Respiratory Society). Refinements in diagnostic algorithms were proposed and validated, increasing the specificity of pre-test clinical probability and d-dimer testing, and thus helping to avoid unnecessary pulmonary angiograms. Improved diagnostic strategies were also successfully tested in pregnant women with suspected PE. Non-vitamin K antagonist oral anticoagulants (NOACs) are now the preferred agents for treating the majority of patients with PE, both in the acute phase (with or without a brief lead-in period of parenteral heparin or fondaparinux) and over the long term. Primary reperfusion is reserved for haemodynamically unstable patients. Besides, the 2019 Guidelines endorse multidisciplinary teams for coordinating the acute-phase management of high-risk and (in selected cases) intermediate-risk PE. For normotensive patients, physicians are advised to include the assessment of the right ventricle on top of clinical severity scores in further risk stratification, especially if early discharge of the patient is envisaged. Further important updates include guidance (1) on extended anticoagulation after PE, taking into account the improved safety profile of NOACs; and (2) on the overall care and follow-up of patients who have suffered PE, with the aim to prevent, detect and treat late sequelae of venous thromboembolism.

## Acute pulmonary embolism: magnitude of the problem

Venous thromboembolism (VTE), clinically presenting as deep vein thrombosis (DVT) or acute pulmonary embolism (PE), is the third most frequent acute cardiovascular syndrome after myocardial infarction and stroke [[1](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR1 "Raskob GE, Angchaisuksiri P, Blanco AN, Buller H, Gallus A, Hunt BJ et al (2014) Thrombosis: a major contributor to global disease burden. Arterioscler Thromb Vasc Biol 34(11):2363–2371")]. Annual incidence rates for PE lie between 39 and 115 per 100,000 population; for DVT, the rates are 53–162 per 100,000 [[2](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR2 "Wendelboe AM, Raskob GE (2016) Global burden of thrombosis: epidemiologic aspects. Circ Res 118(9):1340–1347")]. The incidence of VTE is almost eight times higher in individuals aged 80 years or older than in the fifth decade of life [[2](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR2 "Wendelboe AM, Raskob GE (2016) Global burden of thrombosis: epidemiologic aspects. Circ Res 118(9):1340–1347")]; consequently, and as society’s age, longitudinal studies keep showing a rising tendency in annual PE incidence rates [[3](#ref-CR3 "de Miguel-Diez J, Jimenez-Garcia R, Jimenez D, Monreal M, Guijarro R, Otero R et al (2014) Trends in hospital admissions for pulmonary embolism in Spain from 2002 to 2011. Eur Respir J 44(4):942–950"),[4](#ref-CR4 "Dentali F, Ageno W, Pomero F, Fenoglio L, Squizzato A, Bonzini M (2016) Time trends and case fatality rate of in-hospital treated pulmonary embolism during 11 years of observation in Northwestern Italy. Thromb Haemost 115(2):399–405"),[5](#ref-CR5 "Lehnert P, Lange T, Moller CH, Olsen PS, Carlsen J (2018) Acute pulmonary embolism in a national Danish cohort: increasing incidence and decreasing mortality. Thromb Haemost 118(3):539–546"),[6](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR6 "Keller K, Hobohm L, Ebner M, Kresoja KP, Munzel T, Konstantinides SV et al (2019) Trends in thrombolytic treatment and outcomes of acute pulmonary embolism in Germany. Eur Heart J 41(4):522–529")] over time.

A recent analysis of vital registration data from the World Health Organisation (WHO) Mortality Database (2000–2015) reported an average of 38,929 PE-related deaths each year in 41 states of the WHO European Region (which includes Central Asia) with a total population of approximately 651 million [[7](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR7 "Barco S, Mahmoudpour SH, Valerio L, Klok FA, Munzel T, Middeldorp S et al (2020) Trends in mortality related to pulmonary embolism in the European Region, 2000–15: analysis of vital registration data from the WHO Mortality Database. Lancet Respir Med 8(3):227–287")]. Between 2000 and 2015, annual age-standardised PE-related mortality rates decreased by almost 50% (from 12.7 to 6.5 deaths per 100,000 population) without substantial sex-specific differences. Despite this overall favourable trend, the study also showed (1) that PE-related mortality continues to rise exponentially with age, reaching or even exceeding 80 deaths per 100,000 population among the elderly; and (2) that PE also remains a relatively important cause (compared to other causes) of death among younger women, in whom it accounted for up to 13 cases per 1000 deaths [[7](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR7 "Barco S, Mahmoudpour SH, Valerio L, Klok FA, Munzel T, Middeldorp S et al (2020) Trends in mortality related to pulmonary embolism in the European Region, 2000–15: analysis of vital registration data from the WHO Mortality Database. Lancet Respir Med 8(3):227–287")].

The PE Guidelines of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC), developed in cooperation with the European Respiratory Society (ERS), were updated in 2019 [[8](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR8 "Konstantinides SV, Meyer G, Becattini C, Bueno H, Geersing GJ, Harjola VP et al (2020) 2019 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of acute pulmonary embolism developed in collaboration with the European Respiratory Society (ERS). Eur Heart J 41(4):543–603")]. This article reviews the most important new or changed recommendations along with the recent evidence that provided their rationale and has begun to change clinical practice in several aspects of PE management.

## Refinements in established diagnostic algorithms, and extension of their use to suspected pulmonary embolism in pregnancy

Although the diagnostic steps in the proposed algorithms for the work-up of suspected acute PE have largely remained unchanged since the 2008 ESC Guidelines, refinements continue to be made to increase the specificity of pre-test clinical probability and d-dimer testing with the aim of limiting unnecessary computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA). In particular, the following approaches were successfully validated in recent multicentre management trials:

Since the specificity of d-dimer testing in suspected PE decreases steadily with age [[9](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR9 "Righini M, Goehring C, Bounameaux H, Perrier A (2000) Effects of age on the performance of common diagnostic tests for pulmonary embolism. Am J Med 109(5):357–361")], a multinational prospective cohort study evaluated a previously developed age-adjusted cut-off (age × 10 µg/L for patients older than 50 years) in a cohort of 3346 patients [[10](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR10 "Righini M, Van Es J, Den Exter PL, Roy PM, Verschuren F, Ghuysen A et al (2014) Age-adjusted d-dimer cutoff levels to rule out pulmonary embolism: the ADJUST-PE study. JAMA 311(11):1117–1124")]. Patients with a normal age-adjusted d-dimer value did not undergo CTPA, but were left without anticoagulation and followed for a 3-month period. In patients aged > 75 years, using the age-adjusted (instead of the standard 500 µg/L) d-dimer cut-off increased the number of patients in whom PE could be excluded from 6.4% to 30%, without adding false-negative findings [[10](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR10 "Righini M, Van Es J, Den Exter PL, Roy PM, Verschuren F, Ghuysen A et al (2014) Age-adjusted d-dimer cutoff levels to rule out pulmonary embolism: the ADJUST-PE study. JAMA 311(11):1117–1124")].

Another prospective management trial used the so-called ‘YEARS’ clinical decision rule, which consists of three clinical items of the Wells score, namely signs of DVT, haemoptysis, and ‘PE more likely than an alternative diagnosis’, combined with d-dimer concentrations [[11](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR11 "van der Hulle T, Cheung WY, Kooij S, Beenen LFM, van Bemmel T, van Es J et al (2017) Simplified diagnostic management of suspected pulmonary embolism (the YEARS study): a prospective, multicentre, cohort study. Lancet 390(10091):289–297")]. The diagnosis of PE was rejected without further testing in patients without clinical items and d-dimer levels < 1000 ng/mL, and in patients with at least one clinical item and d-dimers < 500 ng/mL. The remaining patients underwent CTPA. Of the 2946 patients (85%) in whom PE was thus ruled out and who were left untreated, 18 (0.61%, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.36–0.96%) were diagnosed with symptomatic VTE during the 3-month follow-up [[11](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR11 "van der Hulle T, Cheung WY, Kooij S, Beenen LFM, van Bemmel T, van Es J et al (2017) Simplified diagnostic management of suspected pulmonary embolism (the YEARS study): a prospective, multicentre, cohort study. Lancet 390(10091):289–297")]. Using the YEARS rule allowed to exclude PE without CTPA in 48% of the patients as compared to 34% if the original Wells’ rule and fixed d-dimer threshold of less than 500 ng/mL had been applied [[11](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR11 "van der Hulle T, Cheung WY, Kooij S, Beenen LFM, van Bemmel T, van Es J et al (2017) Simplified diagnostic management of suspected pulmonary embolism (the YEARS study): a prospective, multicentre, cohort study. Lancet 390(10091):289–297")].

Based on these results, the guidelines advise to consider either age-adjusted d-dimer cut-offs or the YEARS model as an alternative to the standard interpretation of the d-dimer test with a fixed cut-off level, which also remains a valid option of course [[8](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR8 "Konstantinides SV, Meyer G, Becattini C, Bueno H, Geersing GJ, Harjola VP et al (2020) 2019 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of acute pulmonary embolism developed in collaboration with the European Respiratory Society (ERS). Eur Heart J 41(4):543–603")].

Diagnosis of PE during pregnancy can be challenging as symptoms frequently overlap with those of normal pregnancy. Furthermore, d-dimer levels continuously increase during pregnancy [[12](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR12 "Murphy N, Broadhurst DI, Khashan AS, Gilligan O, Kenny LC, O’Donoghue K (2015) Gestation-specific d-dimer reference ranges: a cross-sectional study. BJOG 122(3):395–400"), [13](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR13 "Ercan S, Ozkan S, Yucel N, Orcun A (2015) Establishing reference intervals for d-dimer to trimesters. J Matern Fetal Neonatal Med 28(8):983–987")] and it has been reported that levels can be above the 500 µg/L threshold in up to 25% of pregnant women in the third trimester [[13](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR13 "Ercan S, Ozkan S, Yucel N, Orcun A (2015) Establishing reference intervals for d-dimer to trimesters. J Matern Fetal Neonatal Med 28(8):983–987")]. Moreover, registry data suggested that d-dimer testing might also be of limited sensitivity in this setting [[14](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR14 "Goodacre S, Horspool K, Nelson-Piercy C, Knight M, Shephard N, Lecky F et al (2019) The DiPEP study: an observational study of the diagnostic accuracy of clinical assessment, d-dimer and chest X-ray for suspected pulmonary embolism in pregnancy and postpartum. BJOG 126(3):383–392")]. Aiming to clarify the situation, a multinational prospective management trial included 441 pregnant women presenting to emergency departments with clinically suspected PE. The results showed that a diagnostic strategy based on the assessment of clinical probability, d-dimer measurement, compression ultrasound of the leg veins, and CTPA may safely exclude PE in pregnancy [[15](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR15 "Righini M, Robert-Ebadi H, Elias A, Sanchez O, Le Moigne E, Schmidt J et al (2018) Diagnosis of pulmonary embolism during pregnancy: a multicenter prospective management outcome study. Ann Intern Med 169(11):766–773")]. A further prospective management study evaluated a combination of a pregnancy-adapted YEARS algorithm with d-dimer levels in 498 women with suspected PE during pregnancy. At 3 months, only one woman with PE excluded on the basis of the algorithm developed a popliteal DVT (0.21%; 95% CI 0.04–1.2) and no woman developed PE [[16](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR16 "van der Pol LM, Tromeur C, Bistervels IM, Ni Ainle F, van Bemmel T, Bertoletti L et al (2019) Pregnancy-adapted YEARS algorithm for diagnosis of suspected pulmonary embolism. N Engl J Med 380(12):1139–1149")]. These results add further support to the pre-existing guidelines’ recommendation to adhere to formal diagnostic assessment with validated methods if PE is suspected during pregnancy or in the postpartum period.

## Risk-adjusted anticoagulation strategies

In patients with high or intermediate clinical probability for PE, anticoagulation should be initiated already upon suspicion and while awaiting the results of diagnostic tests. Parenteral anticoagulation may consist of subcutaneous, weight-adjusted low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) or fondaparinux, or intravenous unfractionated heparin (UFH). However, in haemodynamically stable patients not necessitating thrombolytic, surgical or interventional treatment, anticoagulation can now also be started via the oral route right away, using one of the non-vitamin K antagonist oral anticoagulants (NOAC) apixaban or rivaroxaban. This is in view of phase III clinical trials which demonstrated the non-inferior efficacy and superior safety of a single-oral-drug anticoagulation strategy, using higher doses of apixaban over the first 7 days or rivaroxaban over the first 3 weeks; the comparator arm received the traditional regimen of LMWH over at least 5 days, overlapping with and followed by a vitamin K antagonist (VKA) [[17](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR17 "Agnelli G, Buller HR, Cohen A, Curto M, Gallus AS, Johnson M et al (2013) Oral apixaban for the treatment of acute venous thromboembolism. N Engl J Med 369(9):799–808"), [18](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR18 "Buller HR, Prins MH, Lensin AW, Decousus H, Jacobson BF, Minar E et al (2012) Oral rivaroxaban for the treatment of symptomatic pulmonary embolism. N Engl J Med 366(14):1287–1297")].

Regardless of whether parenteral heparin is used over the first few hours or days after acute PE, the 2019 Guidelines now recommend that, when it is decided to start oral anticoagulation, a NOAC should be preferred to a vitamin K antagonist (VKA) [[8](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR8 "Konstantinides SV, Meyer G, Becattini C, Bueno H, Geersing GJ, Harjola VP et al (2020) 2019 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of acute pulmonary embolism developed in collaboration with the European Respiratory Society (ERS). Eur Heart J 41(4):543–603")]. This strong (class I, A) recommendation is based on the evidence from large clinical trials which led to the approval of three direct coagulation factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, edoxaban, and rivaroxaban) and one thrombin inhibitor (dabigatran) for VTE treatment, and on real-world experience with these drugs which has accumulated since the previous (2014) guidelines. Of note, NOACs should not be given to patients with severe renal impairment, during pregnancy and lactation, and in patients with the antiphospholipid antibody syndrome. The European Heart Rhythm Association has provided and regularly updates a practical guide for the use of NOACs in everyday practice, and for the management of emergency situations related to anticoagulation [[19](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR19 "Steffel J, Verhamme P, Potpara TS, Albaladejo P, Antz M, Desteghe L et al (2018) The 2018 European Heart Rhythm Association Practical Guide on the use of non-vitamin K antagonist oral anticoagulants in patients with atrial fibrillation. Eur Heart J 39(16):1330–1393")].

## Advanced treatment and support of the patient with high-risk and intermediate–high-risk PE

Table [1](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#Tab1) shows the new, extended criteria of haemodynamic instability defining acute high-risk PE, which have been adapted to be in accordance with the criteria used by the other ESC guidelines, notably those on acute and chronic heart failure.

In suspected acute high-risk PE, the clinical probability is usually high, and the differential diagnosis includes other life-threatening situations such as cardiac tamponade, acute coronary syndrome, aortic dissection, acute valvular dysfunction, and hypovolaemia. Immediate bedside transthoracic echocardiography will detect acute RV dysfunction if acute PE is the cause of the patient’s haemodynamic decompensation. In a highly unstable patient, echocardiographic evidence of RV dysfunction is sufficient to prompt immediate reperfusion without further testing. In intubated patients, transoesophageal echocardiography may allow direct visualisation of thrombi in the pulmonary artery and its main branches, especially in patients with RV dysfunction.

The 2019 guidelines recommend to consider setting up a multidisciplinary team for acute-phase management of high-risk and (in selected cases) intermediate-risk PE, depending on the resources and expertise available in each hospital [[8](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR8 "Konstantinides SV, Meyer G, Becattini C, Bueno H, Geersing GJ, Harjola VP et al (2020) 2019 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of acute pulmonary embolism developed in collaboration with the European Respiratory Society (ERS). Eur Heart J 41(4):543–603")]. Primary reperfusion treatment, in most cases systemic thrombolysis, is the treatment of choice for patients with high-risk PE. Surgical pulmonary embolectomy or percutaneous catheter-directed treatment is alternative reperfusion options in patients with contraindications to thrombolysis, if expertise with either of these methods and the appropriate resources are available on site. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) may be life-saving in patients with PE and refractory circulatory collapse or cardiac arrest, but only when used as a bridge to surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed treatment [[23](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR23 "Meneveau N, Guillon B, Planquette B, Piton G, Kimmoun A, Gaide-Chevronnay L et al (2018) Outcomes after extracorporeal membrane oxygenation for the treatment of high-risk pulmonary embolism: a multicentre series of 52 cases. Eur Heart J 39(47):4196–4204")].

In contrast to the clinical setting of high-risk PE, routine use of primary systemic thrombolysis is not recommended in patients with intermediate-risk PE [[24](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR24 "Meyer G, Vicaut E, Danays T, Agnelli G, Becattini C, Beyer-Westendorf J et al (2014) Fibrinolysis for patients with intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism. N Engl J Med 370(15):1402–1411")]. However, patients with intermediate–high-risk PE should be monitored, clinically and haemodynamically, and rescue thrombolytic therapy should be performed in case of overt or imminent haemodynamic decompensation on anticoagulation treatment [[25](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR25 "Marti C, John G, Konstantinides S, Combescure C, Sanchez O, Lankeit M et al (2015) Systemic thrombolytic therapy for acute pulmonary embolism: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Eur Heart J 36(10):605–614")]. As an alternative option, surgical embolectomy or percutaneous catheter-directed treatment should be considered in this latter situation [[8](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR8 "Konstantinides SV, Meyer G, Becattini C, Bueno H, Geersing GJ, Harjola VP et al (2020) 2019 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of acute pulmonary embolism developed in collaboration with the European Respiratory Society (ERS). Eur Heart J 41(4):543–603")].

## Definition of low-risk PE and implications for early discharge and home (outpatient) treatment

Principally, three sets of criteria need to be fulfilled before considering early discharge and home treatment of a patient with acute PE: (1) a low risk of early PE-related life-threatening or serious complications that would require a prolonged hospital stay or (re)hospitalisation; (2) absence of serious comorbidity or aggravating conditions; and (3) the certainty (as much as this is possible) of proper outpatient care and anticoagulant treatment, taking into account the patient’s anticipated compliance, his/her family and social environment, and a local infrastructure permitting rapid access to medical care if necessary.

The PESI, in its original and simplified form (sPESI), integrates clinical parameters of PE severity and comorbidity, and its ability to permit reliable assessment of overall 30-day mortality has been validated in multiple cohorts. Currently, it is the most frequently used tool for risk stratification of acute PE. However, the PESI was not primarily developed as a tool for selecting candidates for home treatment, and it is, therefore, needed to be combined with additional feasibility criteria in a trial which randomised 344 patients to inpatient versus outpatient treatment [[26](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR26 "Aujesky D, Roy PM, Verschuren F, Righini M, Osterwalder J, Egloff M et al (2011) Outpatient versus inpatient treatment for patients with acute pulmonary embolism: an international, open-label, randomised, non-inferiority trial. Lancet 378(9785):41–48")]. Moreover, the sPESI automatically classifies all patients above the age of 80 as well as those with cancer into an ‘elevated risk’ category, but it is not clear whether these patients should a priori be excluded from an early discharge management strategy in the absence of any other criteria of PE severity or serious comorbidity. As an alternative to the (s)PESI, the Hestia exclusion criteria represent a checklist of clinical parameters or questions that can be obtained/answered at the bedside. They integrate PE severity, comorbidity, and feasibility of home treatment. If the answer to one or more of the questions is ‘yes’, then the patient cannot be discharged early. Neither age nor the diagnosis of cancer is among the Hestia criteria. The Hestia criteria safely identified candidates for the early discharge in a single-arm management trial and in a subsequent non-inferiority study [[27](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR27 "den Exter PL, Zondag W, Klok FA, Brouwer RE, Dolsma J, Eijsvogel M et al (2016) Efficacy and safety of outpatient treatment based on the hestia clinical decision rule with or without NT-proBNP testing in patients with acute pulmonary embolism: a randomized clinical trial. Am J Respir Crit Care Med 194(8):998–1006"), [28](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR28 "Zondag W, Mos IC, Creemers-Schild D, Hoogerbrugge AD, Dekkers OM, Dolsma J et al (2011) Outpatient treatment in patients with acute pulmonary embolism: the Hestia Study. J Thromb Haemost 9(8):1500–1507")].

In the context of the physician’s increased responsibility when deciding to send home a patient with an acute cardiovascular syndrome such as PE, the definition of ‘truly low-risk’ PE may require findings beyond those included in clinical scores. This requirement mainly refers to an assessment of RV size, function, and intracardiac thrombi by echocardiography or CTPA. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies supports the notion that the prognostic sensitivity can further be improved when the PESI or sPESI is combined with absence of RV dysfunction on imaging, or with normal laboratory biomarker (mostly troponin) levels [[29](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR29 "Barco S, Mahmoudpour SH, Planquette B, Sanchez O, Konstantinides SV, Meyer G (2019) Prognostic value of right ventricular dysfunction or elevated cardiac biomarkers in patients with low-risk pulmonary embolism: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Eur Heart J 40(11):902–910")]. Furthermore, a multinational prospective management trial investigated the efficacy and safety of early discharge and ambulatory rivaroxaban treatment in patients selected by clinical criteria and the absence of RV dysfunction. Overall, a little less than 20% of the screened unselected patients with PE were included. At the predefined interim analysis of 525 patients (50% of the planned population), the 3-month rate of symptomatic or fatal recurrent VTE was only 0.6%, approximately one-third of the initially estimated rate on the basis of previous studies, and this permitted the early termination of the trial. Major bleeding occurred in 6 (1.2%) of the patients in the safety population. There were no PE-related deaths [[30](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR30 "Barco S, Schmidtmann I, Ageno W, Bauersachs RM, Becattini C, Bernardi E et al (2020) Early discharge and home treatment of patients with low-risk pulmonary embolism with the oral factor Xa inhibitor rivaroxaban. An international multicentre single-arm clinical trial. Eur Heart J 41(4):509–518")].

In view of these data, the 2019 ESC/ERS guidelines recommend to include the assessment of the RV in the risk stratification of all patients with acute PE, on top of the PESI or sPESI score. In particular, the absence of RV dysfunction and right heart thrombi should be ensured before immediate or early (within 24–48 h) discharge of a patient with low-risk PE [[8](/article/10.1007/s11739-020-02340-0#ref-CR8 "Konstantinides SV, Meyer G, Becattini C, Bueno H, Geersing GJ, Harjola VP et al (2020) 2019 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of acute pulmonary embolism developed in collaboration with the European Respiratory Society (ERS). Eur Heart J 41(4):543–603")]. If bedside echocardiography, or a focused ultrasound examination of the heart, is not continuously available at the emergency department of a given hospital, local clinical protocols should request cardiac ultrasound if the CTPA assessment of the RV yields suspicious or inconclusive findings.
